Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verses 1–2:

﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest.﴾ In the language, this fath (conquest, opening) may carry the sense of judgment, meaning: We have given judgment for you over your enemies; or it may be from fath in the sense of bestowal, as in His words: ﴿What Allah grants to people of mercy, none can withhold﴾ [Fatir: 2]; or it may be from the conquest of lands. The scholars differ regarding the intended meaning of this fath, in four opinions.

The first: it is the conquest of Makkah, which Allah promised him before it occurred, and its mention in the past tense is due to its certainty. On this view, it means the conquest of lands.

The second: it refers to what took place at al-Hudaybiyyah, including the Pledge of al-Ridwan and the treaty which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concluded with the Quraysh. On this view, it means judgment or bestowal. What supports the soundness of this opinion is that when the treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah took place, it grieved some of the Muslims because of the conditions it contained, until Allah revealed this surah, showing that this treaty had a praiseworthy outcome. This is the most sound view, because it is related that when these verses were revealed, some people said: "What is this conquest, when the polytheists have barred us from the House?" This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Rather, it is the greatest of conquests. The polytheists have agreed to repel you from their lands with peace, and they have desired from you security."

The third: it refers to the conquests the Muslims achieved after al-Hudaybiyyah, such as the conquest of Khaybar and others.

The fourth: it is guidance to Islam. The evidence for this view is His words: ﴿that Allah may forgive you﴾, where He made the conquest a cause for forgiveness. But there is no proof in this, since it is conceivable that in jihad and other matters there could also be a cause for forgiveness. Alternatively, the lam may indicate becoming and outcome, not causation; so the meaning becomes: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest﴾, and the outcome of your affair was that Allah combined for you the happiness of this world and the Hereafter: He forgave you, completed His favor upon you, guided you, and granted you victory.

﴿It is He who sent down tranquility﴾, that is, calm and serenity, meaning their calm during the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah and their submission to the act of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: its meaning is mercy.

﴿Those who harbour an evil assumption about Allah﴾. Its meaning is that they thought Allah would forsake the believers, and they said: "The Messenger and the believers will never return to their families." It was also said: its meaning is that they do not know Allah through His attributes, and that is the evil assumption about Him. ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾, meaning: you bear witness over your community. ﴿And that you may support him and honor him and revere him﴾. "Ta'zzirūhu" means you honor him, and it was said it means you support him. It is also read as *tu'azziruhu* with two dotted *zāy*s. The pronoun in ﴿*tu'azzirūhu wa tuwaqqirūhu*﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the pronoun in ﴿*tusabbiḥūhu*﴾ refers to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that all three pronouns refer to Allah.

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾, meaning: you bear witness over your community. ﴿And that you may support him and honor him and revere him﴾. "Ta'zzirūhu" means you honor him, and it was said it means you support him. It is also read as *tu'azziruhu* with two dotted *zāy*s. The pronoun in ﴿*tu'azzirūhu wa tuwaqqirūhu*﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the pronoun in ﴿*tusabbiḥūhu*﴾ refers to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that all three pronouns refer to Allah.

This is an honour for the Prophet (ﷺ), in that his pledge of allegiance is placed in the position of the pledge made to Allah. He then emphasised this meaning with His words: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾. This is by way of takhyil (figurative imagery) and tamthil (illustrative representation). He intends that the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which is above the hands of those who pledge allegiance to him, is in meaning the hand of Allah, even though it is not so in reality. What is meant is that the binding of the covenant of allegiance with the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is like binding it with Allah, as in His words: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 80]. Those who interpret (al-mutawwilun) this have taken the hand of Allah to mean His bounty or His power, but this is far-fetched here. The verse was revealed concerning the Pledge of Ridwan (bay'at al-Ridwan) under the tree, which we will mention later. ﴿Whoever breaks it, breaks it only to his own detriment﴾. He means that the harm of his breaking falls upon himself, and by "breaking" (al-nakth) here is meant the annulling of the pledge.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verses 11–12:

﴿The desert Arabs who stayed behind will say to you...﴾ etc.: He named them "those who stayed behind" (al-mukhallafun) because they remained behind from the expedition of al-Hudaybiyah. The Arabs (al-a'rab) are the people of the desert among the Arabs. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Makkah to perform the minor pilgrimage (umrah), they saw that he was heading toward a large enemy from Quraysh and others, so they held back from going out with him. Their faith had not taken firm root, so they assumed that he and the believers would not return from that journey. Allah exposed them in this surah and informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of their words and their excuses before they reached him, and He informed him that they were lying in their excuses: ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾. This may refer to their saying: ﴿Our properties and our families occupied us﴾, since they were lying in that; or to their saying: ﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾, since they said that out of show, without sincerity or repentance. ﴿A people ruined﴾: meaning those who are doomed, from al-bawar, which is destruction; and by it is meant destruction in religion.

﴿The ones left behind will say﴾ and so on. Allah informed His Messenger (ﷺ) that those who stayed behind from the expedition of al-Hudaybiyya wanted to set out with him when he went out on another expedition, which was the expedition of Khaybar. Allah commanded that they be prevented from doing so, and that he say to them: ﴿You will not follow us.﴾ ﴿They want to change the words of Allah﴾, meaning they want to change Allah's promise to the people of al-Hudaybiyya. Allah had promised them that He would compensate them for the spoils of Makkah with the spoils and conquest of Khaybar, and that this would be exclusively theirs and not for others. The ones left behind wanted to share in that with them, and this is what they meant by the change. It has been said that the words of Allah are His saying: ﴿You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me﴾ [At-Tawbah: 83]. This is weak, because this verse was revealed after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk, a considerable time after al-Hudaybiyya. ﴿Thus has Allah said before﴾, meaning His promise of granting the people of al-Hudaybiyya exclusive rights to the spoils of Khaybar. ﴿Then they will say, "Rather, you envy us."﴾ Its meaning: it is difficult for you that we should obtain wealth and spoils along with you. Here, "bal" (rather; a particle of retraction, idrab) is used to turn away from the preceding statement, which is His saying: ﴿You will not follow us; thus has Allah said before﴾. Its meaning is therefore a rejection that Allah had decreed that they should not follow them. As for "bal" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they did not understand except a little﴾, it is a turning away from describing the believers with envy, and an affirmation of describing the ones left behind with ignorance.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verse 16:

﴿You will be called to a people of great military might.﴾ Scholars differed about who these people are, and there are four opinions. The first: they are Hawazin and those who fought the Prophet (ﷺ) at the battle of Khaybar. The second: they are the Romans, since the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called for fighting them at the expedition of Tabuk. The third: they are the people of apostasy (ridda) from Banu Hanifa and others, whom Abu Bakr al-Siddiq fought. The fourth: they are the Persians. The first and second opinions are strengthened by the fact that this happened during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-Mundhir ibn Sa'id strengthened the third opinion, because God made their ruling death or Islam and did not mention the jizya (poll tax). He said: "This applies only to the people of apostasy." I say: it also applies to the disbelieving Arabs, from whom the jizya is not taken. This supports the view that they are Hawazin, or that they will embrace Islam. The phrase ﴿تقاتلونهم﴾ (you fight them) is in the position of a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what precedes it, meaning that ﴿أو يسلمون﴾ (or they submit) is coordinated with it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a new sentence (isti'naf). ﴿And if you turn away as you turned away before﴾ refers to the expedition of Hudaybiyya.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verse 17:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick﴾ (the verse). Its meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, excused the blind, the lame, and the sick for their not going out to jihad, because of their excuses.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verses 18–23:

﴿Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah's will, none of the People of the Tree who pledged allegiance under it will enter the Fire." It is related in a hadith that they were one thousand four hundred, and it was said: one thousand five hundred.

The reason for this pledge (bay'ah) was that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached al-Hudaybiyyah, a place about ten miles from Mecca, he sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) as a messenger to the people of Mecca, to inform them that he had come only to perform 'umrah and that he did not want war. When 'Uthman reached them, his relatives detained him out of honor for him, and then a crier cried out that 'Uthman had been killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then called the people to pledge allegiance to fight and not to flee. It was also said that they pledged allegiance to death. Afterwards 'Uthman came back safe, and a truce was concluded between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people of Mecca, on the condition that he would return that year and perform 'umrah the following year. The tree mentioned was a samurah (acacia) tree there, which later disappeared after some years. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by the site during his caliphate, and the Companions differed about its location.

﴿So He knew what was in their hearts﴾, meaning the sincerity of their faith and the sincerity of their resolve to abide by what they pledged. It was also said: [He knew] their dislike of pledging allegiance to death, but this is false, because it is a censure of the Companions, and we have already mentioned the tranquility (sakinah).

﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾, meaning the conquest of Khaybar. It was also said: the conquest of Mecca, but the first view is more famous. That is, Allah made this a reward for them for the Pledge of Good Pleasure (bay'at al-ridwan), in addition to their reward in the Hereafter.

As for the spoils mentioned first, they are the spoils of Khaybar, and they are conjoined with the near victory. As for the many spoils that Allah promised them, which are mentioned second, they are: everything that the Muslims will gain until the Day of Resurrection. The reference in His words ﴿So He hastened this for you﴾ is to Khaybar. It was also said that the spoils He promised them were Khaybar, and the reference in "this" is to the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah.

﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾, meaning the people of Mecca restrained from fighting you at al-Hudaybiyyah. It was also said: [He restrained] the Jews and others from harming your women and children while you were away at al-Hudaybiyyah.

﴿And that it might be a sign for the believers﴾, meaning this act, namely the restraining of people's hands from you, would be a sign for the believers, by which they would derive evidence of victory. The lam (for "that") is connected to a verb omitted in the text, whose implied meaning is: Allah did that so that it would be a sign.

﴿And other [spoils] you were not able to obtain﴾, meaning the conquest of Mecca. It was also said: the conquest of the lands of Persia and Byzantium. It was also said: the spoils of Hawazin at Hunayn. The meaning is that you were not able to obtain them, but Allah had encompassed them by His power and granted them to you. As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "other" (ukhra), it is either conjoined to "this [spoil]" that He hastened for you, or it is an object of an implied verb whose meaning is: He gave you another, or it is a subject (mubtada').

﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you﴾, meaning the people of Mecca,

﴿[then] the way of Allah﴾, meaning His custom, and the reference is to the Day of Badr. It was also said that the reference is to the victory of the prophets in former times.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then called the people to pledge allegiance to fight and not to flee. It was also said that they pledged allegiance to death. Afterwards 'Uthman came back safe, and a truce was concluded between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people of Mecca, on the condition that he would return that year and perform 'umrah the following year. The tree mentioned was a samurah (acacia) tree there, which later disappeared after some years. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by the site during his caliphate, and the Companions differed about its location.

It was also said: [He knew] their dislike of pledging allegiance to death, but this is false, because it is a censure of the Companions, and we have already mentioned the tranquility (sakinah).

As for the many spoils that Allah promised them, which are mentioned second, they are: everything that the Muslims will gain until the Day of Resurrection. The reference in His words ﴿So He hastened this for you﴾ is to Khaybar. It was also said that the spoils He promised them were Khaybar, and the reference in "this" is to the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah.

﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾, meaning the people of Mecca restrained from fighting you at al-Hudaybiyyah. It was also said: [He restrained] the Jews and others from harming your women and children while you were away at al-Hudaybiyyah.

﴿And that it might be a sign for the believers﴾, meaning this act, namely the restraining of people's hands from you, would be a sign for the believers, by which they would derive evidence of victory. The lam (for "that") is connected to a verb omitted in the text, whose implied meaning is: Allah did that so that it would be a sign.

﴿And other [spoils] you were not able to obtain﴾, meaning the conquest of Mecca. It was also said: the conquest of the lands of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿[then] the way of Allah﴾, meaning His custom, and the reference is to the Day of Badr. It was also said that the reference is to the victory of the prophets in former times.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 48, verse 24:

﴿And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them﴾. It is related concerning its occasion that a group of the youths of Quraysh went out to al-Hudaybiyah, intending to strike at the camp of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against them with a group of the Muslims, and they defeated them and took some of them captive, and brought them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he released them. So the withholding of the hands of the disbelievers was that they were defeated and taken captive. And the withholding of the hands of the believers from the disbelievers was their releasing them from captivity and their being spared from being killed. And His saying: ﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾ means: after you had taken them as captives.

They are the ones who disbelieved, and they barred you from the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), meaning the people of Makkah prevented them from performing the ʿumrah at the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. And the offering (al-hady) detained from reaching its place of sacrifice. Al-hady is what is brought as an offering to the House of livestock animals. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had at that time driven one hundred camels (badanah) to offer, and it was said seventy, in order to present them. Al-maʿkūf means the detained. Its place (mahall) is the place of its slaughter, meaning Makkah and the House. The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of al-hady is that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the object pronoun in ﴿صدوكم﴾, and maʿkūfan is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of al-hady, and an-yablugha is the object of al-ʿakf. So the meaning is: they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and they barred the offering from reaching its place of sacrifice. The ʿakf mentioned here refers to the polytheists' prevention of the offering from reaching Makkah, or the detention of the Muslims with the offering while they looked into their affairs.

﴿And had it not been for believing men and believing women whom you did not know﴾: this verse is the explanation (taʿlīl) for God's turning the believers away from the annihilation of the people of Makkah by killing. That is because in Makkah there were believing men and believing women who concealed their faith. Had God empowered the Muslims over the people of Makkah, they would have killed those believers while not recognizing them. But He restrained them out of mercy for the believers who were among them. The answer to lawlā (the conditional "had it not been for") is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Had it not been for believing men and believing women, We would have given you power over them." ﴿Lest you trample them﴾: it is in the position of a substitute (badal) for "men and women," or a substitute for the object pronoun in "you did not know them." Al-waṭʾ (trampling) here means destruction by the sword and other means. ﴿And there would have befallen you from them a distress﴾: that is, there would have befallen you from their killing hardship and aversion. It is disputed whether this means the sin in killing them, or the blood-money (diyah), or the expiation (kaffārah), or blame, or the disbelievers' reproach of them, by saying: "They killed people of their own religion," or the distress of their souls from killing believers. This last is the most evident, because killing a believer whose faith is unknown while among the people of war carries no sin, no blood-money, no blame, and no reproach. ﴿So that Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾: that is, mercy for the believers who were among the disbelievers, by restraining the swords of the Muslims from the disbelievers for their sake; or mercy for whomever of the disbelievers Allah wills, by their becoming Muslim afterward. The lām is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context of the discourse, and its estimated form is: "The restraint of killing from the people of Makkah was so that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills." ﴿Had they been distinguished, We would have punished those who disbelieved﴾: the meaning of tazayyalū is "separated from the disbelievers." The pronoun refers to the believers whose faith was concealed; that is, had they separated from the disbelievers, We would have punished the disbelievers. So His saying ﴿لعذبنا﴾ is the answer to the second lawlā, and the answer to the first is omitted, as we have mentioned. It is possible that ﴿لعذبنا﴾ is the answer to the first lawlā, and the second lawlā was repeated for emphasis. ﴿When those who disbelieved placed in their hearts ḥamiyyah﴾: that is, the arrogance (anafah) of disbelief, which was their prevention of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims from ʿumrah, and their prevention from writing in the treaty document "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and their prevention from writing "Muhammad, Messenger of Allah." Their saying was: "Had we known you to be the Messenger of Allah, we would have followed you, but write your name and your father's name." The element governing idh (when) in ﴿إذ جعل﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Recall," or His saying ﴿لعذبنا﴾. As-sakīnah is the tranquility and dignity of the Muslims when that occurred. ﴿And He made them adhere to the word of taqwa (piety)﴾: al-Jumhur said it is: "There is no god but Allah," and this has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." It was said: "There is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest." All of these are close in meaning. It was also said: it is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," which the disbelievers refused to have written. ﴿And they were more deserving of it and worthy of it﴾: that is, they were so in the knowledge of Allah and His preordained decree concerning them. It was also said: more deserving of it than the Jews and Christians.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 48, verses 27–28:**

﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had seen in his dream, when he set out for the ʿUmrah, that he and his companions were circumambulating the House, some of them shaving their heads and some of them shortening their hair. It is related that an angel came to him in sleep and said to him: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ (the verse). He informed the people of his vision, and they understood that this would happen in that same year. When the polytheists prevented him from performing ʿUmrah in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) said: "Where is the vision?" Some doubt entered the hearts of the Muslims, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth.﴾ That is, that vision was true, and its interpretation would come to pass afterward. So the hearts of the believers were reassured. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out in the following year, he and his companions, and they entered Makkah and performed ʿUmrah, and they remained in Makkah for three days. The truth of his vision became manifest. That was the ʿUmrat al-Qadiyyah [al-Qaḍāʾ] (the ʿUmrah of fulfilment). Then Makkah was conquered after that, and then he and his companions performed Hajj.

Here, ṣadaqa (to fulfil or to prove true) is transitive to two objects. The phrase bi-l-ḥaqq (in truth) is connected either to ṣadaqa or to al-ruʾyā (the vision), in which case it is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of it.

﴿If Allah wills﴾: Since the exception made by the will of Allah seems to imply doubt about the matter, and doubt is impossible for Allah, scholars differed about this exception in five opinions. The first is that it was an exception spoken by the angel whom the Prophet (ﷺ) saw in the dream, and Allah related his words as they were spoken. The second is that it is a discipline (taʾdīb) from Allah for His servants, so that they say "If Allah wills" concerning every future matter. The third is that the exception refers to each person individually, since it is possible that the matter may be completed for him, or that he may die or fall ill and it will not be completed for him. The fourth is that the exception refers to the words "secure" and not to entering the Mosque. The fifth is that ﴿in shāʾa Allāh﴾ means ﴿idhā shāʾa Allāh﴾ (when Allah wills).

﴿shaving your heads and shortening (your hair)﴾: Shaving (al-ḥalq) and shortening (al-taqṣīr) are part of the sunnah of Hajj and ʿUmrah. Shaving is better than shortening, because of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on those who shave," three times. Then he said the last time: "And on those who shorten."

﴿So He knew what you did not know﴾: This means what He had decreed of the spread of Islam during that period. When the truce was concluded, war was lifted, and people became eager for Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the Battle of al-Ḥudaybiyah with one thousand five hundred men, and it is said one thousand four hundred. He conducted the Conquest (al-Fatḥ) two years after it, with ten thousand men.

﴿So He made, besides that, a near victory﴾: This means the conquest of Khaybar. It is also said that it refers to the Pledge of Ridwan, and it is also said that it refers to the Treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyah. This last is the most sound opinion, because ʿUmar said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is it a victory, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes." It is also said that it refers to the conquest of Makkah, but this is weak, because the meaning of His words ﴿besides that﴾ is before entering the Sacred Mosque, whereas the conquest of Makkah came after that. Al-Ḥudaybiyah was in the sixth year after the Hijrah, the ʿUmrat al-Qadiyyah was in the seventh year, and the conquest of Makkah was in the eighth year.

﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾: This is mentioned in Surat Barāʾah [33].

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾: that is, as a witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, or as a witness to the manifestation of His religion.

As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab), the phrase ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ مَعَهُ﴾ is in apposition to ﴿مُحَمَّدٌ رَّسُولُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ (Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah), and ﴿أَشِدَّآءُ﴾ (fierce) is the predicate about all of them. It was also said that ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ مَعَهُ﴾ is the subject, ﴿أَشِدَّآءُ﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ is the predicate of ﴿مُحَمَّدٌ﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya preferred this view. In my opinion the first view is more likely correct, because the description of being fierce and merciful includes the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions. According to what Ibn 'Atiyya chose, the description of fierceness and mercy would be restricted to the Companions without the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) is more deserving of this description than anyone, since Allah said of him: ﴿compassionate and merciful toward the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. He also said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh toward them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73; al-Tahrim: 9]. This is the fierceness toward the disbelievers and the mercy toward the believers.

﴿سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ﴾ (Their mark is on their faces). The sima (mark, sign) has six interpretations.
The first is that it is the mark that appears on the forehead of the one who prays because of frequent prostration.
The second is that it is the trace of dust on the face.
The third is that it is the paleness of the face from staying awake and worship.
The fourth is the beauty of the face, based on what is reported in a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ). This hadith is not authentic; rather, an error occurred in it, as a narrator raised it to the Prophet (ﷺ) while it is not narrated from him.
The fifth is that it is humility (khushu').
The sixth is that this will be on the Day of Judgment, when Allah places for them a light from the trace of prostration, just as a white mark is placed from the trace of ablution. This is far-fetched, because His saying ﴿تَرَاهُمْ رُكَّعاً سُجَّداً﴾ (You see them bowing and prostrating) describes their condition in this world, so how could their mark on their faces be like that in the Hereafter? The first view is the most evident. Indeed, on the face of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'Ali ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Abbas there was a clear trace of prostration.

﴿ذَلِكَ مَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلتَّوْرَاةِ﴾ (That is their description in the Torah), meaning their description in it. The sentence ends here. Then he begins with His saying ﴿وَمَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلإِنجِيلِ﴾ (and their description in the Gospel), as "like a seed" (كَزَرْعٍ). It was also said that ﴿وَمَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلإِنجِيلِ﴾ is coordinated with ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلتَّوْرَاةِ﴾, and then He begins with ﴿كَزَرْعٍ﴾ (like a seed), and its implied meaning is "they are like a seed." The first view is more evident, so that their description in the Torah is the good qualities mentioned earlier, and their likening in the Gospel is the seed mentioned afterward. On this view, ﴿وَمَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلإِنجِيلِ﴾ means comparison and likeness. On the other view, mathal (description) means attribute, like "their description in the Torah."

﴿كَزَرْعٍ أَخْرَجَ شَطْأَهُ﴾ (like a seed that sends out its shoot). This is a parable Allah struck for Islam, since it began weak and then grew strong and became apparent. It was also said that the seed is a parable for the Prophet (ﷺ), because he was sent alone, and the seed was a single grain, then the Muslims multiplied, so they are like the shoot. The shatʾ is the offshoot of the ear of grain that sprouts around the base. It is said with the ṭāʾ vowelled with sukun and with fatha, with a long vowel and without, and these are different dialects.

﴿فَآزَرَهُ﴾ (then strengthens it) means it made it strong. It is from al-muwazarah, meaning mutual aid. It may be that the subject is the seed and the object is its shoot, or the reverse, since each of them strengthens the other. It was also said that it means it equaled it in height. On this view the subject is the shatʾ, and the form of āzarahu (its verb) is fā'ala. It was also said that it is af'alahu. It was read with a short hamzah, on the pattern fa'ala.

﴿فَٱسْتَغْلَظَ﴾ (then it becomes thick) means it became thick.
﴿فَٱسْتَوَىٰ عَلَىٰ سُوقِهِ﴾ (then stands firm on its stalks): sūq is the plural of sāq (stalk). That is, the seed stood upright on its stalks.

It was also said that His saying ﴿كَزَرْعٍ﴾ (like a seed) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ): he sent out his shoot, Abu Bakr; then it was strengthened by ʿUmar; then it became thick through ʿUthman; then it stood firm on its stalks through ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

﴿لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ ٱلْكُفَّارَ﴾ (that He may enrage the disbelievers by them) is a statement of the reason for what the preceding parable indicates regarding the strength of the Muslims. It is connected to a verb indicated by the context, its implied meaning being: Allah made them so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. It was also said that it is connected to a promise, but this is far-fetched.

﴿مِنْهُم﴾ (from among them) is for specifying the kind, not for partiality, because it is a promise that encompasses all of them, may Allah be pleased with them.
